examples/temperature_sensor_in_a_room/te.description:
#Exercise The true temperature in a room during a given day is
From historic records temperature can extremely vary during a day in the range , and maximum expected temperature changes are of in hour. You have a low quality temperature sensor with of precision that is read every second. Your task is to develop a filter that gives an improved estimation of the real temperature. To that end: Propose a concrete process model out from: Characterize process equation error statistical properties . Deduce maximum variation of temperature in a second, from extreme day temperature variations. Propose a concrete sensor model out from: Characterize the sensor equation error statistical properties . Assume initial conditions and . State is temperature and is approximately constant (varies very slowly) is the error in the hypothesis modeled as a Gaussian white noise with expected maximum temperature change in 1 second. The state is temperature and the model is exact we asume (we leave it in the program as such) that is the equation is exact, but still the sensor measures with noise. Notice that we use this equation as Initial conditions for state Function T__tr=T__tr_func(t) that returns .function T__tr=T__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max) T__tr=(T_max+T_min)/2-(T_max-T_min)/2*sin(t/(24*60*60)*2*pi+pi/2); end Function called T__meas=T__meas_func(t,sigma_T__meas) it adds Gaussian noise to the true temperature with a STD sigma_T__meas. function T__meas=T__meas_func(t,sigma_T__meas,T_min,T_max) T__tr=T__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max); T__meas=T__tr+randn*sigma_T__meas; end Function called z__meas=get_z() return the same that the previous function but has not parameters (uses global) it has an abstract name that allow it to be plugged in an abstract Kalman filter loop.function z__meas=get_z() global t sigma_T__meas T_min T_max z__meas=T__meas_func(t,sigma_T__meas,T_min,T_max); end Try it!. Set t=1789 and sigma_T__meas=4 and call the functionglobal t sigma_T__meas T_min T_max t=1789; sigma_T__meas=4; T_min=18; T_max=28; z__meas=get_z(); Now we have an abstract function independent of the problem type that returns , get_z(). In a general setup we need also a function that returns u=get_u(), but not for this example.global t sigma_T__meas T_min T_max sigma_T__meas=4; T_min=18; T_max=38; global z__tr_func z__tr_func=@(t) T__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max); % mu_x_0 is the initial state estimation mu_x_0=(50-(-5))/2 %ºC % sigma_x_0 is the STD of the initial state estimation sigma_x_0=50-mu_x_0; %ºC sigma2_x_0=sigma_x_0^2; sigma_w=20/(3600) %ºC/s sigma2_w=sigma_w^2 %K^2 sigma_z__meas=[sigma_T__meas] %ºC sigma2_z__meas=sigma_z__meas^2; sigma_v=0; sigma2_v=sigma_v^2 %ºC^2 fid=fopen('sol.dat','w'); mu_x=mu_x_0; sigma2_x=sigma2_x_0; %K^2 t_series=(0:24*3600); t=t_series(1); z__meas=get_z(); fprintf(fid,'%d %d %d %d %d\n',t,mu_x,sigma2_x,z__meas, z__tr_func(t)); for k=1:length(t_series)-1 % Prediction: state @ k+1 using process model mu_x_pred=mu_x; sigma2_x=sigma2_x+sigma2_w; I_x_pred=1/sigma2_x; % Observation: state @ using sensor equation t=t_series(k+1); z__meas=get_z(); mu_x_obs=z__meas; sigma2_x_obs=sigma2_z__meas + sigma2_v; I_x_obs=1/sigma2_x_obs; % Correction: state @ k+1 using ML fusion of estimations I_total=I_x_pred+I_x_obs; mu_x=(mu_x_pred*I_x_pred+mu_x_obs*I_x_obs)/I_total; sigma2_x=1/I_total; fprintf(fid,'%d %d %d %d %d\n',t,mu_x,sigma2_x,z__meas,z__tr_func(t)); end fclose(fid) load -ascii sol.dat ; t_series=sol(:,1); mu_x_series=sol(:,2); sigma2_x_series=sol(:,3); sigma_x_series=sqrt(sigma2_x_series); sigma_z_series=ones(size(sigma_x_series))*sigma_z__meas; z__meas_series=sol(:,4); z__tr_series=sol(:,5); t_series=sol(:,1); fig = figure('visible','off'); plot(t_series,z__meas_series,t_series,mu_x_series,t_series,z__tr_series) title_handle = title("$z^{meas}$ vs $\mu_x$ vs $z^{tr}$"); legend_('$z^{meas}$','$\mu_x$','$z^{t}$') xlabel('$t$'); ylabel('$[^oC]$'); print(fig, 'plot1.png', '-dpng') print(fig, 'plot1.pdf', '-dpdf') fig = figure('visible','off'); plot(t_series,sigma_x_series,t_series,sigma_z_series) title_handle = title("$\sigma_x$ vs $\sigma_{\mu_x}$"); legend_('$\sigma_x$','$\sigma_{z}$') xlabel('$t$'); ylabel('$[^oC]$'); print(fig, 'plot2.png', '-dpng') print(fig, 'plot2.pdf', '-dpdf')

#Exercise The true temperature in a room during a given day is
From historic records temperature can extremely vary during a day in the range , and maximum expected temperature changes are of in hour. You have a low quality temperature sensor with of precision that is read every second. Your task is to develop a filter that gives an improved estimation of the real temperature. To that end: Propose a concrete process model out from: Characterize process equation error statistical properties . Deduce maximum variation of temperature in a second, from extreme day temperature variations. Propose a concrete sensor model out from: Characterize the sensor equation error statistical properties , . Assume initial conditions and . State is temperature plus temperature time derivative: and is approximately constant (varies very slowly) is the error in the hypothesis modeled as a Gaussian white noise with covariance The state is temperature and the model is exact we asume (we leave it in the program as such) but still the sensor measures with noise: . Notice that we use this equation as Initial conditions for state where , with and . Function T__tr=T__tr_func(t) that returns .function T__tr=T__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max) T__tr=(T_max+T_min)/2-(T_max-T_min)/2*sin(t/(24*60*60)*2*pi+pi/2); end Function called T__meas=T__meas_func(t,sigma_T__meas) it adds Gaussian noise to the true temperature with a STD sigma_T__meas. function T__meas=T__meas_func(t,sigma_T__meas,T_min,T_max) T__tr=T__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max); T__meas=T__tr+randn*sigma_T__meas; end Function called z__meas=get_z() return the same that the previous function but has not parameters (uses global) it has an abstract name that allow it to be plugged in an abstract Kalman filter loop.function z__meas=get_z() global t sigma_T__meas T_min T_max z__meas=T__meas_func(t,sigma_T__meas,T_min,T_max); end global t sigma_T__meas T_min T_max t=1789; sigma_T__meas=4; T_min=18; T_max=28; z__meas=get_z(); Now we have an abstract function independent of the problem type that returns , get_z(). In a general setup we need also a function that returns u=get_u(), but not for this example.inject_MATLAB_preamble; global t sigma_T__meas T_min T_max sigma_T__meas=4; T_min=18; T_max=38; global z__tr_func z__tr_func=@(t) T__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max); dz__tr_func=@(t) dT__tr_func(t,T_min,T_max); % mu_x_0 is the initial state estimation T_max_lim=50; T_min_lim=-5; T_0=(T_max_lim+T_min_lim)/2 dT_0=0 %ºC/s mu_x_0=[T_0;0]; % sigma_x_0 is the STD of the initial state estimation % $ \dot{T}^{max}=\frac{20}{3600} ^\circ\text{C/s}$ % $\omega=\frac{2\pi}{24*3600} \text{ rad/s}$ % $\ddot{T}^{max}=\omega \dot{T}^{max}$ sigma_T_0=(T_max_lim-T_min_lim)/2; sigma_dT_0=20/3600 %ºC/s Sigma_x_0=[sigma_T_0; sigma_dT_0] Sigma2_x_0=diag(Sigma_x_0.^2) omega=2*pi/(24*3600) % 2*pi/1 day A_T=(T_max_lim-T_min_lim)/2 Delta_t=1 %s sigma_w_T= 1/2 * 1/sqrt(2) * A_T*omega^2 * Delta_t^2 sigma_w_dT= 10* 1/sqrt(2) * A_T*omega^2 * Delta_t Sigma_w=[sigma_w_T;sigma_w_dT] Sigma2_w=diag(Sigma_w.^2) Sigma_z=[sigma_T__meas] Sigma2_z=diag(Sigma_z.^2); Sigma_v=0; Sigma2_v=Sigma_v^2 fid=fopen('sol.dat','w'); mu_x=mu_x_0; Sigma2_x=Sigma2_x_0; %K^2 t_series=(0:Delta_t:24*3600); t=t_series(1); z=get_z(); f_x=[1,Delta_t; 0,1]; h_x=[1,0]; fprintf(fid,'%d %d %d %d %d %d %d %d\n',t,mu_x,diag(Sigma2_x),z,z__tr_func(t),dz__tr_func(t)); for k=1:length(t_series)-1 % Prediction: state @ k+1 using process model mu_x_pred=f_x*mu_x; Sigma2_x_pred=f_x*Sigma2_x*f_x'+Sigma2_w; i_x_pred=inv(Sigma2_x_pred)*mu_x_pred; I_x_pred=inv(Sigma2_x_pred); % Observation: state @ using sensor equation t=t_series(k+1); z=get_z(); h_x_mu_x_obs=z; Sigma2_h_x_x_obs=Sigma2_z + Sigma2_v; i_x_obs=h_x'*inv(Sigma2_h_x_x_obs)*h_x_mu_x_obs; I_x_obs=h_x'*inv(Sigma2_h_x_x_obs)*h_x; % Fusion: state @ k+1 using ML fusion of estimations I_total=I_x_pred+I_x_obs; mu_x=inv(I_total)*(i_x_pred+i_x_obs); Sigma2_x=inv(I_total); fprintf(fid,'%d %d %d %d %d %d %d %d\n',t,mu_x,diag(Sigma2_x),z,z__tr_func(t),dz__tr_func(t)); end fclose(fid) load -ascii sol.dat ; t_series=sol(:,1); mu_x_series=sol(:,2:3); sigma2_x_series=sol(:,4:5); sigma_x_series=sqrt(sigma2_x_series); sigma_z_series=ones(length(sigma_x_series),1)*Sigma_z; z_series=sol(:,6); z__tr_series=sol(:,7); dz__tr_series=sol(:,8); t_series=sol(:,1); fig = figure('visible','on'); plot(t_series,z_series,t_series,mu_x_series(:,1),t_series,z__tr_series) title_handle = title("$z^{meas}$ vs $\mu_x(1)$ vs $z^{tr}$"); legend_('$z^{meas}$','$\mu_x(1)$','$z^{t}$') xlabel('$t$'); ylabel('$[^oC]$'); print(fig, 'plot1.png', '-dpng') print(fig, 'plot1.pdf', '-dpdf') fig = figure('visible','on'); plot(t_series,mu_x_series(:,2),t_series,dz__tr_series) title_handle = title(" $\mu_x(2)$ vs $\dot{z}^{tr}$"); legend_('$\mu_x(2)$','$\dot{z}^{tr}$') xlabel('$t$'); ylabel('$[^oC]$'); print(fig, 'plot1.2.png', '-dpng') print(fig, 'plot1.2.pdf', '-dpdf') fig = figure('visible','on'); plot(t_series,sigma_x_series(:,1),t_series,sigma_x_series(:,2),t_series,sigma_z_series) title_handle = title("$\sigma_x$ vs $\sigma_{\mu_x}$"); legend_('$\sigma_x(1)$','$\sigma_x(2)$','$\sigma_{z}$') xlabel('$t$'); ylabel('$[^oC]$'); print(fig, 'plot2.png', '-dpng') print(fig, 'plot2.pdf', '-dpdf') fig = figure('visible','off'); plot(t_series,z__tr_series) title_handle = title("$T^{tr}$"); legend_('$T^{tr}$') xlabel('$t$'); ylabel('$[^oC]$'); print(fig, 'plot.png', '-dpng') print(fig, 'plot.pdf', '-dpdf')

information-kalman-filter.html.title: Information Kalman Filter
information-kalman-filter.html.description:
Based on Gaussian Information Aggregation Theorem, assume that we have two sources of information. Process/prediction Equation Sensor/observation Equation We desire to obtain an estimation of , , based on the information provided by the estimate of and estimate of measurements , inputs at two consecutive time steps , and of the modelling errors and . We asume that the knowledge that we have about these variables is statistical even if the underlying physical variable is deterministic ( perspective that we adopt): Noise is Gaussian white, and different noise sources are independent:
We cast these equations so they resemble the form used in Gaussian Information Aggregation Theorem: So, for the process equation:Note that the measurement is obtained through the filter itself, and therefore it is the estimation of the Kalman filter at , : That is, a stochastic variable. Analogously, is the measurement of the input, so it is in general stochastic. Therefore: From which:Notice that is the information coming from the use of the prediction equation; this is addressed making to make explicit the origin of the information.The sensor equation is reordered as: so,Therefore: From which:Notice that is the information coming from the use of the observation equation; this is addressed making to make explicit the origin of the information.Finally, the estimate is: In summary: from which If ( has maximum row rank), then:Notice that this is the estimation of the projection of the state onto the row space of (see figure):
The figure depicts the projection of the state () onto the hyperplane (greenish) expanded by the row space of (). In this way, the estimator can be said to be: "The FIM weighted average of the estimations of the prediction and observation estimations." We can retrieve this interpretation when by splitting the set of observation equations into subsets:where have each one maximum row rank. Now we have several sources of information to aggregate: For each of them Therefore from which Note also that even if , we can write: This equation is a very convenient form to look at the sensor fusion, as it allows to integrate sensors separating them into groups. This can be of interest when having different frequencies for different measurements or predictions of states, or when a sensor or prediction equation may fail. It also makes easy the parallel computation or distribution of the measurements and predictions on different nodes. This robustifies the setup because it easily allows removing different sources of information if they are not available.
